definition: The Office of Communications — the UK regulator for radio spectrum, broadcasting, and telecommunications.
Radio Society of Great Britain — the national amateur radio society, responsible for examinations and training.
A unique identifier assigned to a licensed radio operator, used to identify transmissions on air.
The entry-level UK amateur radio licence, allowing operation at up to 10 watts with a M6 prefix callsign.
V = I × R — the fundamental relationship between voltage (V), current (I), and resistance (R).
Electrical potential difference measured in volts (V). It is the 'pressure' that pushes current through a circuit.
The flow of electric charge measured in amperes (A).
Opposition to current flow measured in ohms (Ω).
A component that stores energy in an electric field. Blocks DC and passes AC. Measured in farads (F).
A component that stores energy in a magnetic field. Opposes changes in current. Measured in henrys (H).
A component that limits current flow. Measured in ohms (Ω).
A semiconductor that allows current to flow in one direction only. Used in rectification (AC to DC conversion).
A semiconductor device used as a switch or amplifier in electronic circuits.
A device that changes AC voltage and current levels using mutual inductance between coils. Only works with AC.
Amplitude Modulation — a modulation method where the amplitude of the carrier wave varies with the audio signal.
Frequency Modulation — a modulation method where the frequency of the carrier wave varies with the audio signal.
Single Sideband — a power-efficient voice mode that transmits only one sideband. USB above 10 MHz, LSB below.
Continuous Wave — Morse code transmission where the carrier is switched on and off. The narrowest bandwidth mode.
A half-wavelength antenna split into two quarter-wave elements, fed at the centre. Impedance approximately 75 Ω.
A directional antenna with a driven element, reflector, and one or more directors. Higher gain than a dipole.
Standing Wave Ratio — a measure of impedance matching between transmitter and antenna. Ideal is 1:1.
Balanced-to-Unbalanced transformer — connects balanced antennas (e.g. dipole) to unbalanced feeders (e.g. coax).
A shielded feeder cable with a centre conductor surrounded by insulation and a braided outer screen. Common types: RG58, RG213.
The way radio waves travel from transmitter to receiver, including ground wave, sky wave, and line of sight.
Layers of ionised gas in the upper atmosphere (D, E, F layers) that can refract HF radio waves back to Earth.
Maximum Usable Frequency — the highest frequency that will be reflected by the ionosphere for a given path.
Radio waves that follow the Earth's surface. Used at MF and lower HF frequencies. Range up to ~100 km.
Radio waves refracted by the ionosphere back to Earth. Enables long-distance HF communication.
Direct wave propagation used at VHF and above. Range limited by antenna height and terrain.
Electromagnetic Compatibility — ensuring electronic equipment does not cause or suffer from radio interference.
Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System — a sub-audible tone sent to activate a repeater or filter unwanted signals.
An automated relay station that receives on one frequency and retransmits on another, extending communication range.
A circuit that silences the receiver audio output when no signal is present, suppressing background noise.
Receiver Incremental Tuning — allows fine adjustment of receive frequency without changing the transmit frequency.
Readability, Signal strength, Tone — the standard reporting system for signal quality. R1–5, S1–9, T1–9.
Standardised three-letter codes beginning with Q, used as shorthand in radio communication (e.g. QTH = location, QRZ = who is calling).
The NATO/ICAO alphabet used to spell out callsigns clearly on air (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, etc.).
Antenna Tuning Unit — a device that matches the impedance of the antenna system to the transmitter for efficient power transfer.
A non-radiating resistive load used for testing transmitters without transmitting a signal on air.
A logarithmic unit for expressing power ratios. +3 dB = double power, +10 dB = ten times power, −3 dB = half power.
High Frequency — the 3–30 MHz band, used for long-distance communication via sky wave propagation.
Very High Frequency — the 30–300 MHz band, used for line-of-sight communication. Includes the 2m amateur band.
Ultra High Frequency — the 300–3000 MHz band. Includes the 70cm amateur band.
The distance a radio wave travels in one complete cycle. Related to frequency by λ(m) = 300 / f(MHz).
The number of complete cycles of a wave per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
A magnetic ceramic material used in chokes and filters to suppress radio frequency interference.
A connection to ground at radio frequencies, used to reduce EMC problems and improve antenna performance.
A general call to all stations, inviting any listener to respond. Used at the start of a contact on both HF and VHF.
A frequency allocation chart showing how each amateur band is divided into segments for different modes and activities.
Direct station-to-station communication on a single frequency, without using a repeater.
Transmitting and receiving on different frequencies, as used when operating through a repeater with a frequency offset.
The unit of electrical power. P = V × I. Foundation licence holders are limited to 10 watts.
A device for transmitting or receiving radio waves. The type and height of antenna greatly affect signal strength and range.
The process of encoding information (voice, data, or Morse) onto a carrier wave. Common types include AM, FM, and SSB.
An unmodulated radio frequency signal generated by an oscillator, onto which information is imposed by modulation.
A circuit or device that increases the strength of a signal. Used in both transmitter (RF power) and receiver (audio) stages.
A circuit that generates a continuous repeating signal at a specific frequency. Used to produce the carrier in a transmitter.
A circuit in a receiver that extracts the original audio or data from a modulated signal. Also called a demodulator.
The audio input level control on a transmitter. Setting it too high causes over-modulation and interference on adjacent channels.
A quarter-wave vertical antenna with radial elements that act as an artificial ground, providing an omnidirectional radiation pattern.
A wire antenna fed at one end, often used on HF. Requires an ATU for matching and can pose a high EMC risk at the feed point.
The orientation of a radio wave — horizontal or vertical. Transmitting and receiving antennas should use the same polarisation.
Opposition to alternating current flow in a circuit, measured in ohms (Ω). Matching impedance between transmitter and antenna is essential for efficient power transfer.
The lowest layer of the ionosphere, present during daytime only. It absorbs and attenuates lower HF signals.
The middle layer of the ionosphere, mainly present during daytime. It can reflect MF and lower HF signals.
The highest ionospheric layer (70–400 km), present day and night. Responsible for long-distance HF propagation.
Q-code meaning 'my location' or 'my address'. Used to share or ask for a station's geographical position.
Q-code meaning 'who is calling me?' Used to ask an unidentified station to identify itself.
Q-code meaning 'I confirm receipt'. Also refers to a QSL card — a written confirmation of a contact between two stations.
Q-code meaning a two-way contact or conversation between amateur radio stations.
The process of converting alternating current (AC) into direct current (DC), typically using one or more diodes.
Light Emitting Diode — a semiconductor component that emits light when forward biased. Used as an indicator in many circuits.
A safety device that melts and breaks the circuit if current exceeds its rated value. Must always be replaced with the correct rating.
A deep tissue burn caused by touching an antenna or feeder carrying RF energy. May not be immediately painful and the full extent can be delayed.
A connection to ground used to provide safety earthing or an RF return path. An RF earth spike near the shack helps reduce EMC problems.
Interference on adjacent channels caused by over-modulation of an AM or SSB transmitter.
The range of frequencies occupied by a transmitted signal. CW has the narrowest bandwidth; FM occupies a wider bandwidth than SSB.
Upper Sideband — the sideband above the carrier frequency. By convention, used for SSB voice communication above 10 MHz.
Lower Sideband — the sideband below the carrier frequency. By convention, used for SSB voice communication below 10 MHz.
The second-tier UK amateur radio licence, allowing up to 50 watts and the ability to build equipment from published designs.
The highest-tier UK amateur radio licence, allowing up to 400 watts and full freedom to design, build, and modify equipment.
Encoding messages so that only intended recipients can read them. Encryption is not permitted under the UK amateur radio licence.
One-way transmission intended for reception by a general audience. Broadcasting is not permitted in amateur radio (CQ calls excepted).
A letter inserted into your callsign to show which part of the UK you are operating from (e.g. W for Wales, M for Scotland). Required when transmitting outside England.
Secondary locator W. Insert after the prefix number (e.g. MW6ABC). Wales has its own amateur radio community and is part of RSGB Region 4.
Secondary locator M. Insert after the prefix number (e.g. MM6ABC). The M stands for 'Modified' — a legacy convention from early UK callsign allocation.
Secondary locator I. Insert after the prefix number (e.g. MI6ABC). The I reflects Ireland, as Northern Ireland shares the island of Ireland.
Secondary locator D. Insert after the prefix number (e.g. MD6ABC). The D derives from the island's Manx name and its distinct Crown Dependency status.
Secondary locator J. Insert after the prefix number (e.g. MJ6ABC). Jersey is a Crown Dependency in the Channel Islands with its own licensing administration.
Secondary locator U. Insert after the prefix number (e.g. MU6ABC). Guernsey is a Crown Dependency in the Channel Islands, separate from Jersey.
No secondary locator is needed when operating from England — use your callsign as issued (e.g. M6ABC). England is the default region in the UK callsign system.
Bayonet Neill-Concelman connector — a small, quick-connect RF connector commonly used on test equipment and some VHF radios.
A large screw-on RF connector (also called a UHF connector) widely used on HF amateur radio equipment. It mates with the SO239 socket.
The panel-mount socket that mates with the PL259 plug. Found on the antenna connection of most HF transceivers and antenna tuning units.
The British Standard for 13-amp mains plugs and sockets used in the UK. Knowing the correct wire colours (Brown=Live, Blue=Neutral, Yellow-Green=Earth) is tested in the Foundation exam.
Protective Multiple Earthing — a mains electricity supply system. You must consult a qualified electrician before connecting an RF earth to a PME supply, as it can create dangerous currents.
Effective Radiated Power — the product of transmitter power and antenna gain. It represents the actual power radiated in a given direction.
A single unit combining both a radio transmitter and receiver. Most amateur radio stations use a transceiver rather than separate units.
Push-To-Talk — a button that switches between receive and transmit. Press to talk, release to listen.
A short burst of 1750 Hz audio tone transmitted to activate older-style amateur repeaters. Newer repeaters typically use CTCSS instead.
Coordinated Universal Time — the global time standard used by amateur radio operators to log contacts, avoiding confusion between time zones.
Radio Frequency — electromagnetic energy in the frequency range used for radio communications, typically from about 3 kHz to 300 GHz.
Medium Frequency — the 0.3 to 3 MHz frequency band. Ground wave propagation works well at MF, and the band includes the 160-metre amateur allocation.
Alternating Current — electric current that periodically reverses direction. UK mains electricity is 230V AC at 50 Hz, and radio signals are a form of AC.
Direct Current — electric current that flows in one direction only. Batteries produce DC, and most amateur radio equipment runs on DC internally.
A material (such as silicon) whose electrical conductivity is between that of a conductor and an insulator. Diodes, transistors, and LEDs are all semiconductor devices.
Radio Teletype — a digital communication mode that sends text characters using frequency-shift keying. One of the oldest digital modes still used on amateur radio.
Phase Shift Keying at 31 baud — a popular digital mode for keyboard-to-keyboard text communication on HF using very narrow bandwidth.
A digital communication mode designed for making contacts under weak-signal conditions. Transmissions last 15 seconds and are decoded by computer.
Long-distance communication, or a distant station. 'Working DX' means making contacts with stations in faraway countries.
The portion of a modulated signal above or below the carrier frequency that carries the actual information. In SSB, only one sideband is transmitted.
Driving the modulator with too much audio, causing the transmitted signal to spread beyond its intended bandwidth and interfere with adjacent channels.
Wire elements extending from the base of a vertical antenna to form an artificial ground plane. A quarter-wave ground plane typically uses four radials.
A parasitic element on a Yagi antenna, slightly shorter than the driven element, positioned in front to focus the radiation pattern forward.
A parasitic element on a Yagi antenna, slightly longer than the driven element, positioned behind it to reflect energy forward and increase gain.
A diagram showing how an antenna radiates energy in different directions. Helps you choose the right antenna for your operating needs.
The intensity of an electromagnetic field at a given point. High field strength near your antenna is a common cause of EMC interference.
Q-code meaning man-made interference on a frequency — disruption from other radio transmissions or electronic equipment.
Q-code meaning natural interference or atmospheric noise (static), typically from thunderstorms.
Q-code meaning low-power operation, typically 5 watts or less. QRP operating is a popular amateur radio activity that tests operator skill.
Q-code meaning 'stop transmitting' or 'I am closing my station'. Used to indicate you are going off the air.
Q-code meaning 'change frequency'. Used to suggest moving the conversation to a different frequency.
A printed postcard-sized confirmation exchanged between amateur operators to verify a contact. Collecting QSL cards is a long-standing tradition.
A designated frequency for making initial contact. After contact, operators move to a working frequency. Examples: 145.500 MHz (2m FM), 433.500 MHz (70cm FM).
The difference between transmit and receive frequencies when using a repeater. On 2m the offset is −600 kHz; on 70cm it is +1.6 MHz.
The 2-metre amateur band (144–146 MHz in the UK), one of the most popular VHF bands for local FM communication and repeater use.
The 70-centimetre amateur band (430–440 MHz in the UK), a popular UHF band for local FM communication, repeaters, and data modes.
The property by which a changing current in one coil induces a voltage in a nearby coil. This is the operating principle behind transformers.
Radiating equally in all horizontal directions. Vertical antennas such as ground planes have omnidirectional radiation patterns.
A measure of how effectively an antenna focuses radio energy in a particular direction compared to a reference, expressed in decibels (dB).
An unintended low-resistance path that allows excessive current to flow. Can cause overheating, fires, or equipment damage.
The final stage of a transmitter that boosts the modulated RF signal to the required output power level before it reaches the antenna.
A circuit in a receiver that increases the demodulated audio signal to a level sufficient to drive a loudspeaker or headphones.
